node.label: Lizabeth Cohen
node.date_label: Making a New Deal (1990) · A Consumers’ Republic (2003) · Saving America’s Cities (2019)
node.description: American social historian whose studies connect workers, consumers, public power and the built environment. Cohen’s interview on Saving America’s Cities explains her shift from ordinary groups to Ed Logue’s public career, retaining attention to social identities and unequal resources. She interprets urban renewal through changing relations between planning experts and community participation, with costs as well as achievements.

named_group_routes.relationship: Against Cohen's technological determinism: the 'material base' is social and historical, and the separation of the economic from the political is specific to capitalism (1981)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Verso repost of NLR I/127 (read in part): Cohen's book is used 'to support an argument against a social interpretation of materialism'; 'what Cohen's technological determinism does is to repeat the error of the political economists: he generalizes the particular historical experience of capitalism'. Callinicos (1990, read): this 'is by no means the first time that Wood has used Brenner's work to distinguish her alternative reading of historical materialism from Cohen's' (p. 111). Brenner (2016): 'Here Ellen's main target was … Gerald Cohen'.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Rule of Freedom (2003): the liberal governance of the nineteenth-century city 'depended on the "rule of freedom"', read through 'maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' in London and Manchester
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Verso description (read 2026-10-22): 'The liberal governance of the nineteenth-century state and city depended on the "rule of freedom"'; the city's 'layout, architecture, infrastructure' and 'such artifacts as maps and censuses, sewers and markets, public libraries and parks' examined for 'the impersonal, often invisible forms of social direction and control built into the infrastructure of modern life'. The body is unread; Cohen (AHR 2004) and Frohman (CJH 2004) are metadata only. Moderate: a publisher's statement of the book's argument.

named_group_routes.relationship: 'The digital revolution has created endless opportunities via blogs, websites, YouTube, and social media' for the historian's stories (2013); presidential columns 'The Public Practice of History in and for a Digital Age' and 'Scholarly Authority in a Wikified World' (2012); 'digital scholarship' named among his fields
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Moderate. The 2013 sentence is read (open AHA text, data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-environment.md §1.3); the 2012 Perspectives columns are known by title from the CV (p. 8) and his AHA-writings page; the CV (p. 1) lists 'digital scholarship' among his fields and (p. 10) the websites he built. The columns themselves are unread. No target strand: the entry's strands are per-work; the coordinator may attach it to the 2005 Cohen–Rosenzweig strand or leave it unattached.

named_group_routes.relationship: Defines cultural history through historically situated meanings, conflicting desires and unintended consequences.
